{{Short description|Statistics concept}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Fano factor''',<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.72.26 | title = Ionization Yield of Radiations. II. The Fluctuations of the Number of Ions | year = 1947 | last1 = Fano | first1 = U. | journal = Physical Review | volume = 72 | issue = 1 | pages = 26–29 |bibcode = 1947PhRv...72...26F }}</ref> like the [[coefficient of variation]], is a measure of the [[statistical dispersion|dispersion]] of a [[counting process]]. It was originally used to measure the [[Fano noise]] in ion detectors. It is named after [[Ugo Fano]], an Italian-American physicist.

The Fano factor after a time <math>t</math> is defined as

:<math>F(t)=\frac{\sigma_t^2}{\mu_t},</math>

where <math>\sigma_t</math> is the [[standard deviation]] and  <math>\mu_t</math> is the mean number of events of a [[counting process]] after some time <math>t</math>. The Fano factor can be viewed as a kind of noise-to-signal ratio; it is a measure of the reliability with which the waiting time [[random variable]] can be estimated after several [[random event]]s.

For a [[Poisson point process| Poisson counting process]], the variance in the count equals the mean count, so <math>F=1</math>.

== Definition ==
For a counting process <math>N_t</math>, the Fano factor after a time <math>t>0</math> is defined as,

:<math>F(t)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(N_t)}{\operatorname{E}[N_t]}.</math>

Sometimes, the long-term limit is also termed the Fano factor,

:<math>F=\lim_{t\to\infty}F(t).</math> 

For a renewal process with holding times distributed similar to a random variable <math>S</math>, we have that,

:<math>F = \lim_{t\to\infty} F(t) = \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{\operatorname{Var}(N_t)}{\operatorname{E}[N_t]} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(S)}{\operatorname{E}[S]^2}. </math><ref>{{cite book|first= D.R.|last= Cox|date= 1962|title= Renewal Theory}}</ref>

Since we have that the right-hand side is equal to the square of the coefficient of variation <math>c_v^2=\operatorname{Var}(S)/\operatorname{E}[S]^2 </math>, the right-hand side of this equation is sometimes referred to as the Fano factor as well.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Shuai |first1= J. W.|last2= Zeng |first2= S. |last3= Jung |first3= P. |date= 2002 |title= Coherence resonance: on the use and abuse of the fano factor| journal= Fluct. Noise Lett.|volume= 02|issue= 3|pages= L139–L146|doi= 10.1142/S0219477502000749}}</ref>

== Interpretation ==
When considered as the dispersion of the number, the Fano factor <math>F</math> roughly corresponds to the width of the peak of <math>N_t</math>. As such, the Fano factor is often interpreted as the unpredictability of the underlying process.

=== Example: Constant Random Variable ===
When the holding times are constant, then <math>F=0</math>. As such, if <math>F\approx0</math> then we interpret the renewal process as being very predictable.

=== Example: Poisson Counting Process ===
When the likelihood of an event occurring in any time interval is equal for all time, then the holding times must be exponentially distributed, giving a [[Poisson point process|Poisson counting process]], for which <math>F=1</math>.

== Use in particle detection ==
In [[particle detector]]s, the Fano factor results from the energy loss in a collision not being purely statistical.  The process giving rise to each individual [[charge carrier]] is not independent as the number of ways an atom may be ionized is limited by the discrete [[electron]] shells.  The net result is a better energy resolution than predicted by purely statistical considerations. For example, if ''w'' is the average energy for a particle to produce a charge carrier in a detector, then the relative [[Full width at half maximum|FWHM]] resolution for measuring the particle energy ''E'' is:<ref name=Leo>{{Cite book |title=Techniques for Nuclear and Particle Physics Experiments: An How-to Approach |url=https://archive.org/details/techniquesfornuc00leow_860 |url-access=limited |first=W.R. |last=Leo |year=1987 |isbn=978-3-540-17386-1 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |pages=[https://archive.org/details/techniquesfornuc00leow_860/page/n119 109]–125}}</ref>
:<math> R = \frac{\mathrm{FWHM}}{\mu} = 2.35 \sqrt{\frac{F w}{E}},  </math>
where the factor of 2.35 relates the standard deviation to the FWHM.

The Fano factor is material-specific. Its value shows an empirical correlation with <math>W/I</math> for gases, <math>F=0.188 W/I - 0.15</math>, where W is the mean energy required to form an ionisation pair and I is the [[ionisation potential]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/231149339 |title=On a relation between the W value and the Fano factor |last=Bronić |first=Ines Krajcar |journal=Journal of Physics B: Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics |volume=25 |number=8 |pages=L215–L218 |doi=10.1088/0953-4075/25/8/004 |year=1992 |bibcode=1992JPhB...25L.215B }}</ref> Some theoretical F values are:<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevB.22.5565 | title = Scattering by ionization and phonon emission in semiconductors | year = 1980 | last1 = Alig | first1 = R. | last2 = Bloom | first2 = S. | last3 = Struck | first3 = C. | journal = Physical Review B | volume = 22 | issue = 12 | pages = 5565 |bibcode = 1980PhRvB..22.5565A }}</ref>

== Use in neuroscience == 
The Fano factor is used in [[neuroscience]] to describe variability in neural spiking. <ref>{{cite book|last1= Dayan|first1= Peter|last2= Abbott|first2= L. F.|date= 2001|title= Theoretical Neuroscience}}</ref> In this context, the events are the neural spiking events and the holding times are the Inter-Spike Intervals (ISI). Often, the limit definition of the Fano factor is used, for which,

<math> F = \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{\operatorname{Var}(N_t)}{\operatorname{E}[N_t]} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(ISI)}{(\operatorname{E}[ISI])^2} = CV^2, </math>

where <math>CV</math> is the coefficient of variation of ISI.

Some neurons are found to have varying ISI distributions, meaning that the counting process is no longer a renewal process. Rather, a [[Markov renewal process]] is used. In the case that we have only two Markov states with equal transition probabilities <math>p</math>, we have that the limit above again converges,<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Ball|first1= F.|last2= Milne|first2= R. K.|date= 2005|title= Simple derivations of properties of counting processes associated with Markov renewal processes}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=October 2025|reason=cited paper, which I believe is doi:10.1239/jap/1134587814 is quite opaque about the  sentence and does not include the following formula}}
<math>F= 2\frac{CV_2^2\mu_1^2 + CV_1^2\mu_2^2}{(\mu_1 + \mu_2)^2} + \left(\frac{1}{p}-1\right)\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{(\mu_1+\mu_2)^2}, </math>
where <math>\mu</math> represents the mean for the ISI of the corresponding state.

While most work assumes a constant Fano factor, recent work has considered neurons with non-constant Fano factors.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Charles|first1=Adam S.|last2= Park|last3= Weller|last4= Horwitz|last5= Pillow|date= 2018|title= Dethroning the Fano Factor: A Flexible, Model-Based Approach to Partitioning Neural Variability|journal=Neural Computation |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=1012–1045 |doi=10.1162/neco_a_01062 |pmid=29381442 |pmc=6558056 }}</ref> In this case, it is found that non-constant Fano factors can be achieved by introducing both noise and non-linearity to the rate of the underlying Poisson process.
